_comment: Evaluation questions for DocuResearch. Each question has a gold answer and passage references. Passage IDs and document IDs are populated from the SQLite content store after ingestion. IDs are deterministic (MD5 hash of filename) so they survive re-ingestion.

questions.text: What encryption algorithm must be used for data transmissions in the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: All data transmissions using the Alpha Protocol must be encrypted with AES-256.

gold_passages.claim: The Alpha Protocol requires AES-256 encryption for all data transmissions.

questions.text: How often must the encryption key be rotated in the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: The encryption key must be rotated every 90 days.

gold_passages.claim: Key rotation must occur every 90 days.

questions.text: Describe the two-step authentication process in the Alpha Protocol.
questions.gold_answer: Authentication in the Alpha Protocol proceeds in two steps. First, the client presents a signed token issued by the identity provider. Second, the server validates the token against the current key registry. If the token is valid and the key has not been revoked, access is granted.

gold_passages.claim: Authentication step one: client presents a signed token from the identity provider.
Authentication step two: server validates the token against the key registry.

questions.text: What is the throughput of the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: The Alpha Protocol achieves a throughput of approximately 10,000 transactions per second on standard hardware.

gold_passages.claim: Throughput is approximately 10,000 transactions per second on standard hardware.

questions.text: What latency can be expected under load for authenticated requests in the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: Latency under load is typically under 50 milliseconds for authenticated requests.

gold_passages.claim: Latency under load is typically under 50 milliseconds for authenticated requests.

questions.text: What are the limitations of the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: The Alpha Protocol does not support multicast transmission. It also cannot be used over connections that do not provide a reliable transport layer.

gold_passages.claim: The protocol does not support multicast transmission.
It cannot be used over connections without a reliable transport layer.

questions.text: What is the most recent version of the Alpha Protocol and when was it published?
questions.gold_answer: The current version is Version 4.0, published on 2025-02-10.

gold_passages.claim: Version 4.0 - 2025-02-10: Current version.

questions.text: What is the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: The Alpha Protocol is a protocol for secure data transmission, first published in 2019.

gold_passages.claim: The Alpha Protocol is for secure data transmission, first published in 2019.

questions.text: Does the Alpha Protocol support multicast transmission?
questions.gold_answer: No, the Alpha Protocol does not support multicast transmission.

gold_passages.claim: The protocol does not support multicast transmission.

questions.text: What programming languages have bindings for the Omega Framework?
questions.gold_answer: The Omega Framework provides bindings for Python, Rust, and Go. The Python bindings are the most widely used.

gold_passages.claim: The Omega Framework provides bindings for Python, Rust, and Go.

questions.text: How does memory management work in the Omega Framework?
questions.gold_answer: Memory management in the Omega Framework is automatic. The framework uses a tracing garbage collector that runs in a background thread, so developers do not need to manually free memory.

gold_passages.claim: Memory management is automatic using a tracing garbage collector in a background thread.

questions.text: What messaging patterns does the Omega Framework support?
questions.gold_answer: The Omega Framework supports two messaging patterns: request-reply and publish-subscribe. The request-reply pattern is synchronous and blocking. The publish-subscribe pattern is asynchronous and non-blocking.

gold_passages.claim: The framework supports request-reply (synchronous, blocking) and publish-subscribe (asynchronous, non-blocking) patterns.

questions.text: What is the maximum throughput of the Omega Framework on a single node?
questions.gold_answer: The Omega Framework can process up to 50,000 messages per second on a single node.

gold_passages.claim: Up to 50,000 messages per second on a single node.

questions.text: How many nodes can the Omega Framework cluster across?
questions.gold_answer: The Omega Framework supports clustering across up to 100 nodes.

gold_passages.claim: Supports clustering across up to 100 nodes.

questions.text: Does the Omega Framework include a built-in service discovery mechanism?
questions.gold_answer: No, the Omega Framework does not include a built-in discovery mechanism. Services must be registered manually or through an external service registry.

gold_passages.claim: No built-in discovery mechanism; services must be registered manually or through an external registry.

questions.text: What is the core API of the Omega Framework?
questions.gold_answer: The core API of the Omega Framework consists of three functions: spawn, send, and receive.

gold_passages.claim: The core API consists of three functions: spawn, send, and receive.

questions.text: When was the Alpha Protocol first published?
questions.gold_answer: The Alpha Protocol was first published in 2019.

gold_passages.claim: First published in 2019.
Revision history: Version 1.0 - 2019-03-15: Initial publication.

questions.text: What is the difference between the Alpha Protocol and the Omega Framework?
questions.gold_answer: The Alpha Protocol is a secure data transmission protocol requiring AES-256 encryption, with key rotation every 90 days, two-step authentication, throughput of ~10,000 transactions/second, and latency under 50ms. It does not support multicast or unreliable transport. The Omega Framework is a distributed systems library with a three-function core API (spawn, send, receive), automatic garbage collection, request-reply and publish-subscribe messaging, up to 50,000 msg/s on a single node, clustering up to 100 nodes, written in C with Python/Rust/Go bindings. The documents do not describe any relationship or comparison between the two -- they are completely separate systems with no documented interoperability or comparative analysis.

gold_passages.claim: The Alpha Protocol is for secure data transmission.
The Omega Framework is a library for building distributed systems.

questions.text: What is the exact key rotation procedure for the Alpha Protocol?
questions.gold_answer: The documents describe only part of the procedure: the encryption key must be rotated every 90 days, and each rotation requires generating a new key pair and securely distributing the public key to all authorized recipients. They do not give an exact step-by-step procedure (for example, how the public key is distributed or how old keys are retired).

gold_passages.claim: Rotation every 90 days; each rotation generates a new key pair and securely distributes the public key.

closest_passage.claim: Key rotation requirements: every 90 days, generate new key pair, distribute public key.

questions.text: What is the Alpha Protocol's maximum supported message payload size?
questions.gold_answer: The documents do not contain any information about the Alpha Protocol's maximum supported message payload size. The closest relevant information is the throughput figure (10,000 transactions per second) and latency figure (under 50ms), but neither addresses payload size limits.

closest_passage.claim: Throughput of ~10,000 transactions per second; latency under 50ms.

questions.text: Which protocol handles automatic memory management: the Alpha Protocol or the Omega Framework?
questions.gold_answer: Only the Omega Framework handles automatic memory management, using a tracing garbage collector in a background thread. The Alpha Protocol is a secure data transmission protocol and the documents describe no memory management for it. The question's premise that either could be the answer does not reflect a disagreement between the sources.

gold_passages.claim: Alpha Protocol is for secure data transmission -- no memory management described.
Omega Framework uses a tracing garbage collector for automatic memory management.

questions.text: When was the Omega Framework first released?
questions.gold_answer: The documents disagree. The Omega Framework documentation says it was first released in 2020, while the Omega Framework release notes say version 1.0 was first released to the public in March 2018.

gold_passages.claim: First released in 2020.
Version 1.0 first released to the public in March 2018.

questions.text: How is "JWT" meant to be pronounced?
questions.gold_answer: The suggested pronunciation of JWT is the same as the English word "jot".

gold_passages.claim: Pronounced like the English word "jot".

questions.text: What does the "exp" claim identify, and how must the current time relate to it?
questions.gold_answer: The "exp" (expiration time) claim identifies the time on or after which the JWT must not be accepted for processing; the current date/time must be before the expiration time.

gold_passages.claim: "exp" identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted; current time must be before it.

questions.text: Is the "exp" claim mandatory, and what kind of value must it contain?
questions.gold_answer: No. Use of the "exp" claim is OPTIONAL. Its value must be a number containing a NumericDate value (implementers may allow a small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, for clock skew).

gold_passages.claim: "exp" identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted; current time must be before it.
Small leeway (usually no more than a few minutes) for clock skew; value MUST be a NumericDate; use is OPTIONAL.

questions.text: What can the "jti" claim be used to prevent?
questions.gold_answer: The "jti" (JWT ID) claim provides a unique identifier for the JWT and can be used to prevent the JWT from being replayed.

gold_passages.claim: "jti" is a unique identifier that can be used to prevent replay.

questions.text: Which signature or MAC algorithms must every conforming JWT implementation support?
questions.gold_answer: Only HMAC SHA-256 ("HS256") and "none" must be implemented. RS256 and ES256 are recommended; other algorithms are optional.

gold_passages.claim: Only HS256 and "none" MUST be implemented; RS256 and ES256 RECOMMENDED.

questions.text: What value is recommended for the "typ" header parameter, and how should it be written?
questions.gold_answer: If present, it is recommended that "typ" be "JWT", always spelled in uppercase for compatibility with legacy implementations. Use of the parameter is optional.

gold_passages.claim: Recommended "typ" value "JWT", uppercase; OPTIONAL.

questions.text: What "alg" header value does an Unsecured JWT use?
questions.gold_answer: An Unsecured JWT uses the "alg" Header Parameter value "none", with the empty string as its JWS Signature value.

gold_passages.claim: Unsecured JWT uses "alg" value "none" and an empty signature.

questions.text: What media type does RFC 7519 register for JWTs?
questions.gold_answer: It registers the "application/jwt" media type.

gold_passages.claim: Registers "application/jwt".

questions.text: Which registered claims represent times, and what format do their values use?
questions.gold_answer: The "exp" (expiration time), "nbf" (not before) and "iat" (issued at) claims. Each value must be a NumericDate: a JSON number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC, ignoring leap seconds.

gold_passages.claim: Small leeway (usually no more than a few minutes) for clock skew; value MUST be a NumericDate; use is OPTIONAL.
"nbf" value MUST be a NumericDate.
"iat" value MUST be a NumericDate.
NumericDate: JSON number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC, ignoring leap seconds.

questions.text: What is a NumericDate in the JWT specification?
questions.gold_answer: A JSON numeric value representing the number of seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC until the specified UTC date/time, ignoring leap seconds; non-integer values can be represented.

gold_passages.claim: NumericDate: JSON number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC, ignoring leap seconds.

questions.text: How long should a JWT remain valid before it expires?
questions.gold_answer: The specification does not recommend a token lifetime. It only defines the "exp" claim (the time after which the JWT must not be accepted) and says implementers may allow a small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, for clock skew. Choosing the lifetime is left to the application.

gold_passages.claim: "exp" identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted; current time must be before it.
Small leeway (usually no more than a few minutes) for clock skew; value MUST be a NumericDate; use is OPTIONAL.

questions.text: What is the maximum size of a JWT in bytes?
questions.gold_answer: The documents do not specify a maximum JWT size.

questions.text: Which JWT libraries does the specification recommend for Python?
questions.gold_answer: The documents do not recommend any libraries or programming languages.

questions.text: How can a JWT be revoked before its expiration time?
questions.gold_answer: The documents do not describe a revocation mechanism. The closest related text is that the "jti" claim can be used to prevent a JWT from being replayed.

closest_passage.claim: Closest: "jti" can be used to prevent replay (not revocation).
